Sherborne
SHUR-burn
n. (the Dorset abbey town and ancient West Saxon see, whose townsmen bought their abbey church at the Dissolution and kept it)
Old English scir burne, the clear stream, from scir, bright or clear, and burna, a brook.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sherborne is the Dorset town that was the seat of the West Saxon bishops from 705, when Aldhelm was made bishop of the western half of Wessex; the see was later divided and finally moved to Old Sarum, leaving Sherborne with a great Benedictine abbey. Two churches stood on the one site, the monks' abbey and the townspeople's parish church of All Hallows, and the arrangement produced a famous quarrel in 1437 in which a parishioner's arrow or a plumber's brazier set the abbey roof alight and burned much of the building; the scorched stone is still visible in the vaulting. At the Dissolution in 1539 the abbey was surrendered and the town bought the abbey church outright and pulled down its own smaller one, so that the townsmen ended with the finer building. The school was refounded by Edward VI in 1550. Sir Walter Raleigh held the castle and estate from 1592. The dictionary records the purchase as the best outcome available from a bad transaction, and marks the difference between a house dissolved for its revenues and a church kept for its use.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an abbey as a monastery; dissolution as the act of breaking up; to surrender as to yield up; a sanctuary as a sacred place; and reverence as fear mingled with respect.

expand to see more

ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion.

DISSOLUTION, n. The act of liquefying; the breaking up of an assembly; destruction of any connected system.

SURRENDER, v.t. To yield to the power of another; to give or deliver up possession upon compulsion or demand.

SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple.

REVERENCE, n. Fear mingled with respect and esteem; veneration; awe of the divine.

Key Scripture

Hag 1:4 — "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

Ezr 3:12 — "But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy:"

Psa 74:7 — "They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground."

Hab 2:20 — "But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him."

Modern Corruption

Dorset town and ancient West Saxon see whose abbey burned in a quarrel with its own parishioners in 1437 and whose townsmen bought the abbey church at the Dissolution and kept it for the parish.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the Dissolution as it was actually conducted, and the dictionary names it without pretending the monasteries were innocent. The houses were suppressed, their lands sold and their plate melted, and the proceeds went to the crown and to the gentry rather than to preaching, schools or the poor; the reform that was pleaded for was not the reform that was carried out. Haggai's rebuke falls on exactly this order of priorities, asking “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). The psalmist's lament over a sanctuary handled roughly is not a defence of the monks' religion but a warning about the handling: “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7), and Sherborne's own vaulting had been scorched once already in 1437 by a quarrel among Christians.

The second paragraph records what was done well here, because the dictionary is bound to say so. The town did not loot the abbey; it bought the church and used it, and demolished its own lesser building rather than keep two. That is the right instinct about a building: it is for the worship of God by a congregation, not a monument to be venerated or a quarry to be stripped. Ezra marks the mixed feeling proper to such a moment, when the old men who had seen the first house “wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy” (Ezr 3:12), grief and gladness together. And the rule for what is to happen inside the walls, whoever built them, is Habakkuk's: “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chareb (H2720), waste or desolate; Hebrew miqdash (H4720), a sanctuary; Hebrew hekal (H1964), a temple or palace.

expand to see more

Hebrew chareb (H2720) — dried up, waste, desolate; “and this house lie waste?”, Haggai 1:4.

Hebrew sapan (H5603) — to cover or panel with boards, to ceil; “to dwell in your cieled houses”, Haggai 1:4.

Hebrew miqdash (H4720) — a consecrated place, a sanctuary; “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary”, Psalm 74:7.

Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to defile; “they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place”, Psalm 74:7.

Hebrew hekal (H1964) — a large building, a temple; “But the LORD is in his holy temple”, Habakkuk 2:20.

Usage

"“and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4) — abbey revenues to the crown and the gentry, 1539."

"“wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy” (Ezr 3:12) — the townsmen buying the abbey church."

"“let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20) — the use a kept building is for."
